title: The Guest Star: July 1054
eyes: Astronomical Bureau of the Song court (Sitiandian / Sitianjian)
Liao (Khitan) court record, as preserved in the Qidan guozhi
Anonymous author of the Tractatus de ecclesia S. Petri Aldenburgensi
Unknown Ancestral Puebloan painter(s) of the Peñasco Blanco panel
Nicholas U. Mayall and Jan H. Oort (with J. J. L. Duyvendak)
places: Rome (as reported in a Flemish text)
Kyoto (the event; copied in the 13th century)
Peñasco Blanco, west end of Chaco Canyon, New Mexico
Constantinople, the patriarchate at Hagia Sophia
Observatory in the tower of the Hôtel de Cluny, Paris
intro: Before dawn on 4 July 1054 (Julian), astronomers of the Song court at Kaifeng logged a new star a few inches, in their angular measure, from Tianguan, the star now called zeta Tauri, at the tip of the Bull's southern horn. For twenty-three days it could be seen in full daylight, as bright as Venus, with points of light on four sides and a reddish-white colour. By night it lingered for almost two years, until the bureau reported on 6 April 1056 that the 'guest' had left. The star had exploded about 6,500 light years away; its debris is the Crab Nebula, and the collapsed core at its centre was found in 1968 to be a pulsar spinning about thirty times a second. This chapter is unusual in Many Eyes because almost none of its eyes is a diary in the modern sense. The East Asian records are official astronomical and court documents, and most survive only inside compilations made long afterwards: the Song shi was compiled in 1343–45, the Song huiyao survives as a nineteenth-century reconstruction, the Liao record sits in a thirteenth-century history of the Khitan, and the Japanese entries were copied from the archive of the Onmyōryō (the court Bureau of Yin and Yang) into Fujiwara no Teika's diary in 1230 and into the chronicle Ichidai yōki. The one possible witness from the Mediterranean, the physician Ibn Butlan, is known only through a biographical dictionary compiled two centuries later. Each eye's form and authenticity notes say plainly what kind of record it is and how it reached us. The records disagree in instructive ways. The Japanese texts put the star in the fourth month, which would place it in May, when Taurus was lost in the Sun's glare; most scholars read this as a copying error for the fifth month. One Chinese compilation gives the day as yichou instead of jichou, which would move the first sighting to 10 June. A Liao text links the star to a solar eclipse and to the death of the Khitan emperor. A minority of modern researchers have argued from European and Near Eastern texts that the star appeared in April or May, earlier than the Chinese date; others reject every European candidate. In the American Southwest, a painted hand, crescent and star below the Peñasco Blanco great house in Chaco Canyon has been read since 1955 as a record of the star beside the waning Moon on 5 July 1054, and is also firmly doubted. These are laid out here as positions, not settled facts. Twelve days after the first sighting, on Saturday 16 July 1054, the papal legate Cardinal Humbert of Silva Candida walked into Hagia Sophia in Constantinople and laid a bull excommunicating Patriarch Michael Cerularius on the altar. If the Chinese date is right, the guest star was then still visible in the daytime sky above the city. No Greek or Latin writer of the schism mentions it. title: The Long-Haired Star: Spring 1066
eyes: Anonymous scribes of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (versions C and D)
Designer and embroiderers of the Bayeux Tapestry
Astronomers of the Song Astronomical Bureau
Astronomical officials of the Goryeo court
Japanese court observers and diarists (Heian period)
Compiler of the Rus' Primary Chronicle (Povest' vremennykh let)
Irish annalists (Annals of Ulster; Annals of the Four Masters)
places: Isle of Wight and the south coast
intro: In the spring of 1066 the comet now named after Edmond Halley swung around the Sun (perihelion fell around 20–23 March) and passed unusually close to the Earth in late April, at roughly a tenth of the Earth–Sun distance. For about two months it was one of the most conspicuous objects in the sky from Ireland to Japan. It rose first as a dawn object in the east, then vanished into the Sun's glare. Around 24 April it reappeared in the evening sky in the north-west with a long tail, and it faded through May into early June. No one who saw it kept a diary in the modern sense. The honest record is made of annals, chronicles, an official astronomical register and one embroidered strip of linen, and the form tags say so. Some of it is close to contemporary: the Chinese bureau's daily positions, the English chronicles kept at Abingdon and Worcester, William of Jumièges writing in Normandy within a few years. Much of it was written down later: Zonaras and Matthew of Edessa in the twelfth century, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn al-Athir in the late twelfth and early thirteenth, the Goryeosa in 1451, the Annals of the Four Masters in the 1630s. Each eye carries a note on when its words were set down. The heart of the chapter is the week of 24 April. The Chinese astronomers at Kaifeng logged the comet's return as a white vapour, then measured a tail more than ten degrees long. The English scribes wrote that it was first seen on the eve of the Greater Litany and shone for seven nights. The Irish annals put it on the Tuesday after Low Sunday, and a Norman monk saw a three-forked tail in the north-west. Japanese courtiers saw it in the west at dusk. In each place it was read through local expectations. To the Song bureau it was a broom star to be measured against the lunar lodges. The Rus' chronicler saw blood in its rays. To an old monk at Malmesbury it was a scourge to England. On the ground, the year was crowded. Edward the Confessor died on 5 January and Harold Godwinson was crowned the next day. Tostig raided the English coast soon after the comet's week. Harald Hardrada and Tostig fell at Stamford Bridge on 25 September. William of Normandy landed at Pevensey three days later, won at Hastings on 14 October and was crowned on Christmas Day. Later writers bent the comet towards these events. The Bayeux Tapestry sets it just after Harold's coronation, months before it actually appeared. One Norman poem moves it to the autumn landing. These rearrangements are set out here as positions, beside the dated sky. The eastern records do something the western ones do not. They give lodge-by-lodge positions and dates that modern astronomers have used to check the comet's orbit, and Kevin Yau's reconstruction suggests that the April positions imply a perihelion two or three days later than the tabulated date. The same sky that frightened kings has become data.

title: Halley's Eclipse: 3 May 1715
eyes: Unnamed keeper of the Alkborough parish register
places: At sea near the Canary Islands
The Royal Society's house in Crane Court, Fleet Street, London
Alkborough, north Lincolnshire, near the Humber
intro: On the morning of 22 April 1715, by the Julian calendar England still kept, the Moon's shadow came in from the Atlantic over Cornwall and Devon, swept north-east across the Midlands and East Anglia, and went out over the North Sea towards Scandinavia. London lay inside the band of totality. It was the first total eclipse visible in the south of Britain for centuries; the printed notices of the day spoke of five hundred years. What makes the day unusual is that it was announced. In March 1715 Edmond Halley, Savilian Professor of Geometry at Oxford and Secretary of the Royal Society, had John Senex engrave and sell a sixpenny broadsheet map showing the shadow's path over England, with a note telling the public that the darkness was natural and not an omen against the new Hanoverian king, and asking 'the Curious' to time the total darkness with pendulum clocks. William Whiston, the dismissed Lucasian professor, sold a rival calculation through the same engraver. Pamphleteers sold threepenny tracts with titles like The Black-Day, or a Prospect of Doomsday. Halley's request worked. Reports came back from clergymen, gentlemen and professors along and beside the track: Wanstead, Greenwich, Upminster, Oxford, Cambridge, Barton by Kettering, King's Walden, Witley, Norton Court in Kent, Haverfordwest. Halley printed them in the Philosophical Transactions with the durations each place measured, and from the spread of numbers drew the real edges and centre line of the shadow. A second paper gathered accounts from abroad: a mariner at sea off the Canaries, a list of German cities, and a professor at Uppsala who saw over four minutes of totality and the winter stars at noon. Two Frenchmen, the Chevalier de Louville and Pierre Rémond de Montmort, crossed the Channel to watch from the Royal Society's house in Crane Court. Because Halley's request asked for the same quantity everywhere, the record of this eclipse is less a set of diaries than a coordinated experiment: each eye here is a timed report, a letter, a printed map, a parish register or a collector's dated note. The chapter lays them in order of place along the shadow and of time across the following months, when Halley published a corrected map 'as it was observed' and, in 1723, reused the plate for the next eclipse. The same sheet of sky also carried older readings. A parish register in Lincolnshire set the eclipse down as a warning to the world; Whiston, late in life, called it a divine signal. Halley's broadsheet had been written precisely against such readings. The eyes here therefore disagree not only about how many seconds the darkness lasted, but about what it meant.

title: The Night the Stars Fell: 12–13 November 1833
places: At sea off the Florida Keys
Camp on the Missouri River bottoms, between Jackson and Clay counties, Missouri
Aboard ship off the Florida Keys
intro: In the last hours before dawn on Wednesday 13 November 1833, the sky over most of North America filled with meteors. From New England to the Gulf, and west across the Mississippi to the Plains, people woke to a sky in which streaks of light fell faster than anyone could count, for two or three hours, until daylight drowned them. Modern estimates put the rate in the tens of thousands per hour. The night was clear and cold almost everywhere, so almost everyone east of the Rockies who was awake, or was woken, saw the same thing at the same moment. What they made of it depended on who they were. In New Haven the Yale professor Denison Olmsted noticed that the meteors seemed to stream from one point among the stars of Leo, and that the point moved with the stars, not with the Earth. He asked the public, through the newspapers, to send him their observations, and turned what came back into the first long scientific study of a meteor shower. In Kirtland, Ohio, Joseph Smith wrote in his journal that the falling stars fulfilled scripture. On the Eastern Shore of Maryland a fifteen-year-old enslaved boy, Frederick Bailey, later Frederick Douglass, watched at daybreak and wondered if the Son of Man was coming. On the bank of the Missouri, Latter-day Saint families just driven out of Jackson County took the sky as a sign in their favour. On the northern Plains, Lakota and Nakota keepers of winter counts gave the whole winter of 1833–34 its name from the night. The record is mixed, and the form tags say so. Smith's journal entry was written within days. The newspapers were printed within a week or two. Olmsted's and Alexander Twining's papers in the American Journal of Science appeared in 1834. Douglass's account was written twenty-two years later, in his 1855 memoir, and Parley Pratt's in an autobiography published in 1874. The winter counts are pictographic records dated by winter rather than by day, recorded by Garrick Mallery and other collectors decades later. Testimonies of formerly enslaved people collected by the WPA in the 1930s, and an anecdote that Abraham Lincoln, then in Illinois, later retold the night during the Civil War (it reaches us second-hand, through Walt Whitman), are a full century or a generation removed and are not used here as entries. The night had a forerunner. On 12 November 1799 Alexander von Humboldt and Aimé Bonpland at Cumaná, on the coast of what is now Venezuela, and the American surveyor Andrew Ellicott, at sea off the Florida Keys, saw the same kind of storm. In 1833 a North Carolina paper reprinted a description of the Cumaná display beside its own. Thirty-one years later Hubert Anson Newton of Yale, working through old chronicles, found the storms returned about every thirty-three years and predicted one for November 1866. It came, over Europe. title: The Carrington Storm: 28 August – 4 September 1859
eyes: The New York Times (reporters and correspondents)
Officers of the deck, USS Saranac and USS Sabine
La Sociedad (Mexico City newspaper) and its Querétaro correspondent
S. E. Bishop (identified as Sereno Edwards Bishop)
Author of the Chikusai Nikki (diarist known as Chikusai)
Sydney Morning Herald and Moreton Bay Courier
places: USS Sabine, off Greytown, Nicaragua (about 11°32′ N)
Boston and Portland, Maine (American Telegraph Co.)
Philadelphia–Pittsburgh and South Braintree–Fall River lines
Kew Observatory, Old Deer Park, Richmond
New York and New Haven, gathering letters from the Americas and beyond
Boston, collecting reports from lines across New England and beyond
Mexico City, with a correspondent at Querétaro
Montería, on the Sinú river, about 8°45′ N
intro: On the evening of Sunday 28 August 1859 the sky over New England, the Caribbean and, a few hours later, south-eastern Australia turned red. Telegraph lines from Quebec to Pittsburgh behaved as if a hand were opening and closing the circuit; at Kew, outside London, the self-recording magnetographs began to draw jagged traces. That was the first storm. Four days later came a second and greater one, and in between, just before noon in Surrey on 1 September, two amateur astronomers saw something no one had described before: a burst of white light on the face of the Sun itself. Richard Carrington at his private observatory at Redhill and Richard Hodgson at Highgate each saw the flare at about 11:18 Greenwich time, and each saw it fade within about five minutes. At almost the same moment the Kew instruments, in Balfour Stewart's care, recorded a sharp small disturbance. Roughly seventeen and a half hours later the magnetic field across the whole Earth was thrown into disorder. Over the night of 1–2 September aurorae were seen overhead in Havana and Mexico, from ships off Nicaragua, in Santiago de Chile, on Maui, and the next evening in Japan and Melbourne. In Bombay the Colaba magnetometer recorded a fall in the horizontal field later estimated at about 1,600 nanotesla, and the Rome and Greenwich instruments ran off their scales. Almost none of this record is a diary in the strict sense, and the chapter says so. The eyes here are two astronomers' notes to the Royal Astronomical Society; an observatory's photographic traces and the paper written on them; two compilers, Elias Loomis at Yale and the telegraph engineer George Prescott in Boston, who gathered eyewitness letters from hundreds of places; newspaper columns from New York, Sydney, Brisbane and Mexico; deck logs of United States Navy ships; a missionary's letter from Lahaina; a colonial telegraph superintendent's report to Parliament; a scientist's observing book in Melbourne; a merchant-scholar's diary in Ise province; and, from Colombia, a parish priest's account whose date is disputed. Read side by side, they make the shape of the event visible. The same red glow that the officer of the deck on the Saranac logged at four in the morning at Panama was being described as 'blood-red' in Sydney at seven in the evening, at very nearly the same instant. Telegraphers in Boston and Portland, Maine, and in Victoria, Australia, found on the same storm that they could unplug their batteries and send messages on the sky's current alone. And observers who could not have known of each other, in Ise, on Maui and in Montería, first took the light for a distant fire. The interpretation was contested from the start. Carrington refused to claim that the flare caused the storm, warning that one coincidence proved nothing; Stewart, writing in 1861, was willing to suggest that the Sun had been caught in the act. title: Tunguska and the White Nights: 30 June 1908
eyes: Evenki herders near the epicentre (Chuchancha, Chekaren and others)
Kirensk correspondent of the newspaper Sibir' (Irkutsk)
Kezhma correspondent of the newspaper Krasnoyarets
places: Chum on the Avarkitta, some tens of km from the centre
Porch of his house, Vanavara trading post
Ridge north of the Makirta, looking north
Southern Swamp, centre of the forest-fall
Camps on the Avarkitta and other streams some tens of kilometres from the centre of the forest-fall
Porch of his house at the Vanavara trading post, about 65 km SSE of the centre
Reporting from Nizhne-Karelinskoye, about 30 versts north of Kirensk
Kirensk, on the Lena, roughly 400–500 km ESE of the centre

intro: Shortly after seven in the morning local time on 30 June 1908 (17 June by the Russian calendar), something from space blew apart several kilometres above the taiga north of the Podkamennaya Tunguska river in central Siberia. Seismic reckoning puts it at about 00:14 GMT. No crater was ever found. What was found was a forest knocked flat across hundreds of square kilometres, its trunks lying in a radial pattern pointing away from a centre where trees still stood, stripped and scorched. Evenki herders camped within a few tens of kilometres were thrown from their tents. At the Vanavara trading post, about 65 km to the south-south-east, a man sitting on his porch felt a heat as if his shirt were on fire, and was knocked to the ground. This is a chapter of records rather than diaries. Nearly everything from Siberia in 1908 survives as short newspaper reports, letters from meteorological observers, and police and post-office replies collected by the Irkutsk observatory. The most vivid accounts, from the Evenki and from Vanavara, were written down only in the 1920s and 1930s, by the ethnographer Innokenty Suslov and the meteorite hunter Leonid Kulik, nearly twenty years after the event. Where testimony was recorded later, the entries say so. Newspaper and observer dates from 1908 are in the Russian Old Style calendar and are converted here. The same sky reached far beyond Siberia. The pressure wave crossed Eurasia and was traced by microbarographs in England about five hours after the blast. It was recognised for what it was only in 1930, when F. J. W. Whipple at Kew matched the British traces to the Siberian fall. The seismograph at Irkutsk, some 970 km away, recorded the ground shaking for well over an hour; stations at Tashkent, Tiflis and Jena also wrote it down. Then came the nights. From the evening of 30 June, and for a few nights after, the northern sky over Europe and western Russia stayed light. People in England sat sewing out of doors after ten at night and read print after midnight. Letters went to The Times and to Nature. Almost nobody in Europe connected the light to Siberia. Astronomers and editors argued for aurora, for high luminous clouds, or for dust like that thrown up by Krakatoa in 1883. Some observers, such as W. F. Denning and the Prussian meteorologists, noted that the twilights were already unusual for some days before 30 June. That point is still argued: some modern authors tie the whole optical anomaly to the incoming body, others suggest part of it was unrelated. The chapter sets these out as positions. The second half of the chapter belongs to Kulik. He first went east in 1921 for the new Soviet Academy of Sciences, gathering accounts at Kansk and Kezhma. In April 1927 he finally looked out from a ridge over the felled forest. Further seasons in 1928 and 1929–30 dug and drilled in the swampy hollows of the centre, looking for a buried iron mass that was never there. title: Through the Tail: Halley's Comet, 1909–1910
eyes: American newspapers (New York Times, San Francisco Examiner and others)
places: New York and San Francisco newsrooms
Kodaikanal Observatory, Palani Hills, Madras Presidency
intro: Halley's comet was the first comet to return on schedule because someone had said it would. By 1909 its next perihelion had been computed to within days, and observatories on every inhabited continent were sweeping the predicted place with photographic plates. On 11 September 1909 Max Wolf at Heidelberg found it on one, a smudge far too faint for the eye. In Egypt, Harold Knox-Shaw soon discovered that a plate he had taken on 24 August already held it. Then the sky played a trick. In mid-January 1910 a different comet, unpredicted and far brighter, blazed out of the southern dawn. Miners in the Transvaal are thought to have seen it first, and Robert Innes in Johannesburg studied it as it rounded the Sun in daylight. Many who later said they remembered Halley's comet of 1910 were probably remembering this one, the Great January Comet. The chapter keeps the two apart. In February the Yerkes spectrographs found cyanogen in Halley's comet, and a New York reporter's call to Camille Flammarion turned a spectral band into a poison cloud. Through the spring the press sold fear and mocked it in the same pages: comet pills, comet insurance, comet parties. Meanwhile astronomers explained, mostly in smaller print, that a comet's tail is thinner than any laboratory vacuum. Mark Twain, born in 1835 a fortnight after the comet's last perihelion, died on 21 April 1910, the day after its next one, as he had said he would. Edward VII died in London on 6 May, while the comet hung in the morning sky. The heart of the chapter is the night of 18–19 May, when Earth was expected to pass through the tail. It is set beside the weeks either side, when the world's observatories worked almost as one instrument: Yerkes and Lowell, Mount Wilson and its outpost on Diamond Head in Honolulu, Kodaikanal in south India, Helwan in Egypt, Johannesburg, Tokyo, and an old amateur at Windsor, New South Wales. E. E. Barnard's published observing journal is the backbone: dated, candid about smoke and haze, careful about what he could not prove. Most of these eyes are not diarists in the private sense. They speak through observing journals, plates, spectra, press statements and newspapers, and the form tags say so. Several important records could not be consulted directly, among them the Times's original pages and the Transvaal circulars; where the chapter relies on later studies it says which. What the record shows is a public expecting an event and a profession that, on the night itself, measured almost nothing out of the ordinary and said so.

title: Light Bent: The Eclipse of 29 May 1919
eyes: Andrew Claude de la Cherois Crommelin
Brazilian newspapers: Estado do Pará, Correio da Semana, Jornal do Commercio
G. M. Harvey and the Royal Greenwich Observatory astrometry group (led by Andrew Murray)
places: Roça Sundy, north-west Príncipe, Portuguese West Africa
Jockey Club ground, Sobral, Ceará, Brazil
Royal Greenwich Observatory, Herstmonceux Castle, Sussex
intro: On 29 May 1919 the Moon's shadow crossed the Atlantic from Brazil to the Gulf of Guinea. The Sun stood in front of the Hyades, a cluster rich in bright stars, and for five or six minutes those stars could be photographed beside the darkened limb. If Einstein's general theory of relativity was right, their light would be bent by the Sun's gravity by 1.75 seconds of arc at the limb. A Newtonian reckoning gave half that, and no bending at all was also possible. Two British parties were sent to catch the shadow. Arthur Eddington and the clockmaker E. T. Cottingham went to the Portuguese cocoa island of Príncipe. Andrew Crommelin and Charles Davidson of Greenwich went to Sobral in the Brazilian state of Ceará. The plan was Frank Dyson's, the Astronomer Royal, who had pointed out the opportunity in 1917, in the middle of a war, for a theory published by a German professor in Berlin. Eddington was a Quaker who refused military service. His deferment was bound up with the expedition. The parties sailed together from Liverpool in March 1919 while the Paris peace conference was still sitting. On the day, Príncipe was clouded after a morning thunderstorm and yielded only a few usable plates. Sobral cleared a minute before totality, but the main astrographic telescope had shifted focus in the heat. The smaller 4-inch lens, a reserve instrument, gave the sharpest images. This chapter is built from dated letters, telegrams, expedition reports, a field diary, newspaper pages and the published record of a meeting. It holds almost no diaries in the strict sense, and the form tags say so. Eddington's letters to his mother and sister are at Trinity College, Cambridge. Davidson's diary is in the Greenwich archives and is unpublished. Einstein's postcard to his mother and Lorentz's telegram are in the Collected Papers of Albert Einstein. All of these are given as digests only. The 1920 report in the Philosophical Transactions is a pre-1929 English text and is quoted in short phrases. The Brazilian side was not a backdrop. Henrique Morize, director of the Observatório Nacional in Rio, had recommended Sobral in 1918 and led his own eight-member commission there to study the solar corona. The Belém newspaper Estado do Pará printed a translated article by the British astronomers in April 1919. Sobral's diocesan weekly and the Rio press carried the story on. Príncipe was a Portuguese colony worked largely by contract labourers from Angola and elsewhere. The eclipse was observed from the Roça Sundy plantation, but no Príncipe voice from that day has been traced for this chapter. The final eyes are later readers of the same plates. At the joint meeting of the Royal Society and the Royal Astronomical Society on 6 November 1919, Ludwik Silberstein urged caution. The next morning The Times announced a revolution in science.
